L10:

L15: cite6†View PDF cite7†HTML (experimental) L16: > Abstract:We present a framework for verifying the deterministic structured computations surrounding a large language model rather than the model itself, extending a Lean 4 trust-boundary architecture to the generic interfaces of modern LLM pipelines.
L17: Certificate validity is a Lean 4 kernel type-check plus a sorry-free transitive axiom audit against the trusted set {propext, cite8†this http URL†classical.choice , cite9†this http URL†quot.sound }; other assumptions are declared and partitioned by tier (mathematical placeholders, cryptographic assumptions, ML/human oracles).
L18: > The technical contribution comprises three local certificate families and two operators. The families are conflict-aware bilattice grounding (with an emission-gate soundness lemma), embedding sensitivity and paraphrase stability, and Hoare-style agent action.
L19: The operators are a Maximal Certifiable Residue, which turns abstention into the maximum-weight certifiable residue with audit-logged dropped claims, and a Compositional Stability theorem, which yields a closed-form pipeline-wide perturbation budget from per-layer gains and margins.
L20: The three families plus a Universal Assurance Card consolidator form the per-call deliverable for high-stakes deployments: patent and legal retrieval, regulated finance, clinical decision support, and agentic systems with irreversible side effects.
L21: > A compiled Lean 4 reference artifact (Lean v4.30.0-rc2, Mathlib) covers all 22 certificate types, with 17 of 46 kernel-audited declarations axiom-free, the rest depending only on the trusted set and declared assumptions, and zero uses of sorryAx or cite10†this http URL†lean.ofreducebool .
L22: The three families are empirically tested through four registered pilots: bilattice grounding on adversarially perturbed HotpotQA, embedding sensitivity in short- and long-form settings, and Hoare-style agent action on a filesystem sandbox with adversarial prompt injection.

L9: # Title:The Test Oracle Problem in Synthetic LLM-as-Judge Corpora: Disappearance, Distortion and a Validation Protocol
L10: 
L11: Authors:cite5†Serkan Ballı (Department of Software Engineering, Mehmet Akif Ersoy University, Burdur, Türkiye)
L12: 
L13: View a PDF of the paper titled The Test Oracle Problem in Synthetic LLM-as-Judge Corpora: Disappearance, Distortion and a Validation Protocol, by Serkan Ball{\i} (Department of Software Engineering and 3 other authors
L14: 
L15: cite6†View PDF cite7†HTML (experimental) L16: > Abstract:Studies of bias in LLM-as-judge systems typically build synthetic corpora by prompting an LLM to generate a hallucinated answer to pair with a factual one, then presenting both to a judge. We report a case in which this generation step silently failed, and use it to argue that the failure mode is structural rather than incidental.
L17: In a multilingual (Turkish/English) faithfulness-judgment corpus, a decoding-budget parameter shared between judging and generation calls truncated one producer's hallucinated answers to a few words. The resulting items produced a large, statistically robust effect: a 32-point cross-lingual collapse in one judge's selection accuracy, replicated from N=50 to N=500, explained by a three-layer mechanistic account, and confirmed by a controlled producer-swap experiment, none of which was real.
L18: The effect vanished to ceiling once the shared parameter was corrected, and only manual reading of the raw generations, not any aggregate statistical check, exposed the fault. A second measured bias (Markdown-formatting preference) was not fabricated but distorted by the same fault, its magnitude and in one case its sign shifting with stimulus length, a mode aggregate metrics cannot distinguish from the first.
L19: We frame the underlying vulnerability using the test oracle problem: corpora whose negative examples are LLM-generated carry no mechanical way to verify item integrity, while corpora built by deterministic perturbation of a gold answer carry an item-level oracle for free. A positive control supports this claim directly: an analogous fault injected into a minimal perturbation-based corpus is caught with 100% accuracy by a zero-cost, zero-human gold-to-negative string comparison.
L20: We close with a validation protocol, derived from our own case, for analysts working in the oracle-less regime that we argue describes most contemporary multilingual LLM-as-judge corpora.

L113:                        JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS)
L114: 
L115:     Abstract
L116: 
L117:        Cryptographic operations like hashing and signing need the data to be
L118:        expressed in an invariant format so that the operations are reliably
L119:        repeatable.  One way to address this is to create a canonical
L120:        representation of the data.  Canonicalization also permits data to be
L121:        exchanged in its original form on the "wire" while cryptographic
L122:        operations performed on the canonicalized counterpart of the data in
L123:        the producer and consumer endpoints generate consistent results.
L124: 
L125:        This document describes the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS).  This
L126:        specification defines how to create a canonical representation of
L127:        JSON data by building on the strict serialization methods for JSON
L128:        primitives defined by ECMAScript, constraining JSON data to the
L129:        Internet JSON (I-JSON) subset, and by using deterministic property
L130:        sorting.

L190:     1.  Introduction
L191: 
L192:        This document describes the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS).  This
L193:        specification defines how to create a canonical representation of
L194:        JSON [RFC8259] data by building on the strict serialization methods
L195:        for JSON primitives defined by ECMAScript [ECMA-262], constraining
L196:        JSON data to the I-JSON [RFC7493] subset, and by using deterministic
L197:        property sorting.  The output from JCS is a "hashable" representation
L198:        of JSON data that can be used by cryptographic methods.  The
L199:        subsequent paragraphs outline the primary design considerations.
L200: 
L201:        Cryptographic operations like hashing and signing need the data to be
L202:        expressed in an invariant format so that the operations are reliably
L203:        repeatable.  One way to accomplish this is to convert the data into a
L204:        format that has a simple and fixed representation, like base64url
L205:        [RFC4648].  This is how JSON Web Signature (JWS) [RFC7515] addressed
L206:        this issue.  Another solution is to create a canonical version of the
L207:        data, similar to what was done for the XML signature [XMLDSIG]
L208:        standard.
L209: 
L210:        The primary advantage with a canonicalizing scheme is that data can
L211:        be kept in its original form.  This is the core rationale behind JCS.
L212:        Put another way, using canonicalization enables a JSON object to
L213:        remain a JSON object even after being signed.  This can simplify
L214:        system design, documentation, and logging.
L215: 
L216:        To avoid "reinventing the wheel", JCS relies on the serialization of
L217:        JSON primitives (strings, numbers, and literals), as defined by
L218:        ECMAScript (aka JavaScript) [ECMA-262] beginning with version 6.
L219:        Seasoned XML developers may recall difficulties getting XML
L220:        signatures to validate.  This was usually due to different
L221:        interpretations of the quite intricate XML canonicalization rules as
L222:        well as of the equally complex Web Services security standards.  The
L223:        reasons why JCS should not suffer from similar issues are:
L224: 
L225:        *  JSON does not have a namespace concept and default values.
L226: 
L227:        *  Data is constrained to the I-JSON [RFC7493] subset.  This
L228:           eliminates the need for specific parsers for dealing with
L229:           canonicalization.
